title: GuardMem AI
tagline: A memory governance gateway for long-running AI agents
overview: Every candidate fact an agent wants to remember is intercepted before it becomes durable state. GuardMem extracts structured claims anchored to verbatim source spans, validates them against a tenant ontology, scores confidence and blast-radius risk on separate axes, and then auto-writes, queues for human review, rejects, or escalates. Every decision lands in a hash-chained audit log.
challenges: Stopping confabulation at the door: no verbatim source span, no write.
Separating confidence (semantic entropy over meaning clusters) from impact risk (blast radius) so a confident write to a high-stakes field still escalates.
Fail-closed degradation: provider outage, budget cap or injection detection all route toward human review and never widen the auto-write path.
Never deleting beliefs: supersession plus tombstones with bitemporal columns make 'what did the agent believe on date X' a normal query.
architecture:
raw turns
   |
   v
[L1 EXTRACTION]  noise -> candidates + verbatim spans
   |
   v
[L2 VALIDATION]  ontology | NLI contradiction | cardinality | temporal overlap
   |
   v
[L3 SCORING]     C (semantic entropy)   R (blast radius)
   |
   v
[DECISION] --> AUTO_WRITE | HITL_REVIEW | REJECT | ESCALATE
   |
   v
Postgres txn + hash-chained audit events

title: Enterprise HR Agentic RAG Copilot
tagline: Agentic RAG that grades its evidence, or refuses to answer
overview: A Forward Deployed Engineer style project that takes a RAG notebook to a deployable internal HR product. An 11-node LangGraph agent routes, grades retrieved evidence, rewrites queries, falls back to cited web search, and finally declines. Around it sit the layers that make it a product rather than a demo: hybrid BM25 + dense retrieval fused by reciprocal rank fusion and re-ranked, a supervisor-worker team of six specialists with handoff and escalation, a ReAct loop over a tool registry, input and output guards with PII redaction, role-based authorization, a human-in-the-loop approval queue, loop budgets, model routing with a cost projection, a semantic cache, SSE streaming and span tracing. Every answer is logged to an audit trail the browser console renders. The public demo runs with no API keys at all - retrieval degrades to BM25 over the policy documents on disk and answers come from an extractive path that cannot invent a number - and a visitor can paste their own OpenAI or Groq key for written answers.
status: Live on Vercel; DigitalOcean deploy and feedback capture pending
challenges: Making 'internal policy does not cover this' a reachable outcome, not a fallback nobody wired up.

Calibrating the 0.15 relevance gate from a 12-question benchmark so it rejects every out-of-domain chunk and drops no real one - a wrong-source chunk still scored 0.521, which is why an LLM grader sits behind the gate rather than instead of it.

Keeping the product answerable with no credentials at all, so the degradation ladder ends in an extractive answer that is structurally incapable of inventing a policy number rather than in an apology.

Finding the failures that were silent: a complexity classifier inverted in both directions at once, and three configuration switches that did nothing - an empty semantic cache was falsy, so the test guarding it skipped both the lookup and the store.

title: Latent Instability Diagnostics (LID)
tagline: Detect LLM hallucinations one token before they are emitted
overview: Every mainstream hallucination detector is post-hoc. LID measures how sensitive a model's hidden-state manifold is to controlled Gaussian perturbation, flagging a tipping point 1 to 2 tokens ahead of the first hallucinated token. Eight baselines are reproduced behind a unified API for a fair comparison.
challenges: Formalising instability as I(l,t) magnitude divergence plus q(l,t) directional alignment, combined into a composite score Z.
Keeping cost to 15-20% on one consumer GPU by re-projecting perturbed states through a stateless lm_head with 8-bit per-token tracing.
Reproducing DoLa, Semantic Entropy, LSD, SSP, INSIDE, SEP and ITI under one harness.
Making every figure regenerable by one command behind a 1,250-line pytest suite.
architecture:
prompt -> LLM decode step t
            |
            v
   hidden state h_l(t)
      |            \
      |   + Gaussian noise (sigma = alpha * RMS(h))
      v            v
   h_clean       h_pert
        \          /
   I = ||dh|| / ||h||    q = cos(h_clean, h_pert)
               |
               v
      Z = w*I + (1-w)*(1-q)
               |
   peak > mean(Z) + 1.5*std(Z)  -->  flag BEFORE token t+1

title: Maryland UI Pulse
tagline: Are Maryland's unemployed paid within 21 days? A live US map, benchmark and forecast
overview: An independent analytics project on how quickly Maryland pays first unemployment insurance benefits, benchmarked against every US jurisdiction using public US Department of Labor data. It ships as a live interactive web app with a state map, trend explorer, delay distribution, claims forecast and what-if slider, plus a Power BI report, static dashboards and a Q&A. Maryland pays 72.5% of first payments within 21 days against an 87% federal standard, 48th of 53.
challenges: Working out an undocumented federal file: the ETA 9050 column layout had to be inferred, and an early double-count was caught by checking against the Department's own published chart (Maryland 69.3% and US 83.4% for 2025, 14.1% in June 2020).
Separating volume from lateness: late payments average about 1,600 a month whether claims rise or fall (correlation 0.01), which points to process bottlenecks rather than intake capacity.
Being honest about what public data cannot show: backdating cannot be separated from agency delay, correlations are descriptive, and the forecast is illustrative.

One pipeline, several audiences: a live web app, a Power BI project and .pbix, static dashboards and state maps, all rebuilt from two public files, with a tone that treats the Department's challenges as context, not blame.

title: AI Engineering Roadmap 2026
tagline: A 19-chapter, code-first guide to production AI engineering, delivered as a Netflix-style reading app
overview: An open-source guide to building reliable, measurable and secure LLM systems: 19 chapters and 187 concept sections covering prompting, structured output, embeddings and RAG, evaluation, agents, fine-tuning, serving, safety and CI/CD. Every concept follows one four-part arc (deep dive, cross-connections, production anti-patterns, minimal working code). It ships as Markdown, per-chapter PDFs and a zero-dependency streaming-style web app with role-based profiles, a resume-where-you-left-off reader, My List and search. A structural audit and a published cross-check report document what is verified and what is not.
challenges: Keeping 'comprehensive' honest: the audit script enforces the four-part format, parses every Python block and checks about 170 required concepts, but it cannot judge correctness, so the repo ships a CROSSCHECK.md listing what is unexecuted, thin or perishable instead of claiming completeness.

Making code claims verifiable: every section that needs only the standard library or NumPy was executed in a clean directory (144 ran). Two apparent failures turned out to be artifacts of running via python -c, and 35 library-dependent sections are syntax-checked only, which the README says plainly.

A reading experience that does not need a framework: chapters render client-side, poster art is generated as seeded SVG graphs, and progress lives in localStorage with no tracking. A Vercel deployment-protection setting and a git-triggered build from the wrong root directory briefly caused a 404 and had to be diagnosed and fixed.
One source of truth: Markdown chapters feed the PDFs, the audit and the site data through scripts, so the three outputs cannot drift apart.

   +--> [build_pdfs.py] markdown + xhtml2pdf -> pdfs/

   +--> [build_site_data.py] chapters + PDFs + section index -> site/data.js

[Static web app] profiles | hero | rows | reader (resume) | search

Vercel (static, security + cache headers)

title: Energy Price Forecasting with Macro and News Signals
tagline: WTI crude oil and Henry Hub gas forecasts from FRED indicators and GDELT news features
overview: A GWU Data Science capstone comparing ARIMA, SARIMA, SARIMAX, LSTM and CNN+LSTM models across price-only, macro-only, news-only and fused news-plus-macro inputs at daily and monthly frequency. Evaluation is walk-forward, and the repo holds a Streamlit demo, a LaTeX report and a research paper. Built as a two-person team; the repo is a fork of the teammate's, where Vishal made 79 commits.
challenges: Isolating what each information source adds: the report finds GDELT news is weak alone (MAPE 107% for gas with news only) but helps when fused with macro variables.
Results are mixed rather than uniformly in favour of deep learning: univariate SARIMA has the lower monthly gas RMSE (0.376) and classical daily models are competitive.
Interpreting short held-out windows, where R2 can go negative because of low variance in the test slice rather than a useless forecast.
Keeping daily and monthly data aligned (forward-fill, monthly resampling, first differencing for stationarity) under one walk-forward protocol.

overview: A personal experiment repo implementing several LangGraph workflows: three RAG variants, a SQL agent over a sample employee database, a multi-agent system combining SQL, web search, YouTube search and a calculator, and human-in-the-loop approval with structured outputs. It is a learning playground rather than a product, with no evaluation numbers.

metrics.label: Multi-agent tools
metrics.value: SQL, web search, YouTube search, calculator

challenges: Routing a question to the right tool in the multi-agent graph.
Recovering from irrelevant retrieval, which Corrective RAG and Self-RAG handle by re-checking or rewriting the query.
Keeping a human in control with an approval step before answers are finalised.
Not benchmarked: the repo has no quantified evaluation.
architecture:
question
   |
   v
[LangGraph router]
   |
   +--> RAG: agentic | corrective | self (query rewrite)
   +--> tools: SQL | web search | YouTube | calculator
   |
   v
[human approval] --> structured answer

title: LLMOps Interview Preparation
tagline: Production LLMOps curriculum: 20 modules, serving, guardrails, observability and evaluation, as an Amazon-style reading app
overview: A senior-level LLMOps curriculum: inference serving (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM), vector databases, guardrails, tracing and evaluation, agents and MCP, and QLoRA fine-tuning triggers. 20 modules and 142 concept episodes include runnable code and staff-level scenarios, and ship as a static web app with role-based profiles and search.

metrics.label: Executed in a clean directory
metrics.value: 83 sections ran, 0 failed (15 need third-party libs)

challenges: Keeping the claims honest: a published cross-check report lists what is executed, syntax-checked only, or perishable.
